An isonormal Gaussian map built from independent Gaussian coordinates

References and publication status for this development

Paper references

The two step-size regimes and the coefficient 1.651.651.65 follow Theorem 1(a)–(b) of Dalalyan and Karagulyan (2019). Dalalyan (2017), Theorem 1 and Section 6, gives the earlier synchronous-coupling argument.

  • Arnak S. Dalalyan and Avetik G. Karagulyan (2019). User-friendly guarantees for the Langevin Monte Carlo with inaccurate gradient. Stochastic Processes and their Applications 129(12), 5278–5311. arXiv
  • Arnak Dalalyan (2017). Further and stronger analogy between sampling and optimization: Langevin Monte Carlo and gradient descent. Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Learning Theory, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 65, 678–689.

Let ι\iotaι be an arbitrary index set and let Q=⨂i∈ιN(0,1)Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)Q=⨂i∈ι​N(0,1) be the product of standard Gaussian laws on Ω=Rι\Omega=\mathbb R^\iotaΩ=Rι, the space of all real families ω=(ωi)i∈ι\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in\iota}ω=(ωi​)i∈ι​. Under QQQ the coordinates ξi(ω)=ωi\xi_i(\omega)=\omega_iξi​(ω)=ωi​ are independent standard Gaussian random variables, so their classes ZiZ_iZi​ in the Hilbert space L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q) form an orthonormal family. Consequently, for every square-summable family of coefficients a=(ai)∈ℓ2(ι)a=(a_i)\in\ell^2(\iota)a=(ai​)∈ℓ2(ι) the series S(a)=∑iaiZiS(a)=\sum_ia_iZ_iS(a)=∑i​ai​Zi​ converges in L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q), and ∥S(a)∥22=∑iai2\|S(a)\|_2^2=\sum_ia_i^2∥S(a)∥22​=∑i​ai2​.

Let HHH be a real Hilbert space with a Hilbert basis (bi)i∈ι(b_i)_{i\in\iota}(bi​)i∈ι​. Composing the coordinate map x↦(⟨bi,x⟩)i∈ιx\mapsto(\langle b_i,x\rangle)_{i\in\iota}x↦(⟨bi​,x⟩)i∈ι​ with SSS gives a linear isometry Ib:H→L2(Q)I_b:H\to L^2(Q)Ib​:H→L2(Q), Ib(x)=∑i⟨bi,x⟩ZiI_b(x)=\sum_i\langle b_i,x\rangle Z_iIb​(x)=∑i​⟨bi​,x⟩Zi​. We prove that every Ib(x)I_b(x)Ib​(x) has mean zero and law N(0,∥x∥2)\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)N(0,∥x∥2), and that Cov⁡(Ib(x),Ib(y))=⟨x,y⟩\operatorname{Cov}(I_b(x),I_b(y))=\langle x,y\rangleCov(Ib​(x),Ib​(y))=⟨x,y⟩ for all x,y∈Hx,y\in Hx,y∈H; a linear map with these properties is called an isonormal Gaussian map. Finite partial sums of the series are Gaussian because finite sums of independent Gaussian variables are Gaussian; the infinite sums are Gaussian because a centred Gaussian law whose variance is the squared L2L^2L2 norm is preserved under limits in L2L^2L2, which is proved with characteristic functions.

The construction assumes no previously given Gaussian process. In the following sections the joint Gaussianity of finitely many values of IbI_bIb​ is deduced from linearity, and IbI_bIb​ is applied to the indicator functions 1(0,t]\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}1(0,t]​ in L2L^2L2 of Lebesgue measure to obtain a Brownian motion.

Statement and proof

01The product of standard Gaussian laws §

Mathematical statement and proof

Definition. Let ι\iotaι be an arbitrary index set (finite, countable or uncountable) and let Ω=Rι\Omega=\mathbb R^\iotaΩ=Rι be the set of all families ω=(ωi)i∈ι\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in\iota}ω=(ωi​)i∈ι​ of real numbers. Equip Ω\OmegaΩ with the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra F\mathcal FF, the smallest σ\sigmaσ-algebra for which every coordinate map ξi:Ω→R\xi_i:\Omega\to\mathbb Rξi​:Ω→R, ξi(ω)=ωi\xi_i(\omega)=\omega_iξi​(ω)=ωi​, is Borel measurable. Let N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1) be the standard Gaussian law on R\mathbb RR, with density (2π)−1/2e−x2/2(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}(2π)−1/2e−x2/2. The source measure is the product probability measure

Q=⨂i∈ιN(0,1)on (Ω,F).Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\qquad\text{on }(\Omega,\mathcal F).Q=i∈ι⨂​N(0,1)on (Ω,F).

It is the unique probability measure on F\mathcal FF such that, for every finite set F⊆ιF\subseteq\iotaF⊆ι and all Borel sets Ai⊆RA_i\subseteq\mathbb RAi​⊆R (i∈Fi\in Fi∈F),

Q({ω∈Ω: ωi∈Ai for all i∈F})=∏i∈FN(0,1)(Ai).(1)Q\bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega:\ \omega_i\in A_i\text{ for all }i\in F\}\bigr)=\prod_{i\in F}\mathcal N(0,1)(A_i).\qquad(1)Q({ω∈Ω: ωi​∈Ai​ for all i∈F})=i∈F∏​N(0,1)(Ai​).(1)

The existence of such a measure for an arbitrary family of probability measures is the theorem on infinite products of probability measures, a consequence of the Kolmogorov extension theorem. Uniqueness holds because the sets on the left of (1), the measurable cylinders, are closed under finite intersections and generate F\mathcal FF, so that Dynkin's π\piπ-λ\lambdaλ theorem applies. The properties of QQQ used below (total mass one, the laws of the coordinates and their independence) all follow from (1). No countability of ι\iotaι is assumed anywhere in this section.

How the Lean proof follows this argument

The definition source sets source ι equal to Measure.infinitePi (fun _ : ι ↦ gaussianReal 0 1), a measure on the function type ι → ℝ, which carries the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra. Mathlib's gaussianReal m v is the real Gaussian law with mean mmm and variance vvv; the variance has type ℝ≥0 (nonnegative reals), and for v=0v=0v=0 the measure is the Dirac mass at mmm. Mathlib's Measure.infinitePi is the product of an arbitrary family of probability measures, characterised as the unique probability measure that gives every finite box the product of the masses of its sides; this is property (1). The family here is constant, so every factor is N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1), and the index type ι is an arbitrary type, as in the definition.

02The source measure has total mass one §

Mathematical statement and proof

Claim. Q(Ω)=1Q(\Omega)=1Q(Ω)=1; that is, QQQ is a probability measure.

Proof. Apply (1) with F=∅F=\varnothingF=∅. The condition imposed on ω\omegaω is then vacuous, so the set on the left of (1) is Ω\OmegaΩ, and the right-hand side is the empty product, which equals 111. □\square□

Consequently bounded measurable functions are QQQ-integrable, constant functions belong to L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q), and L2(Q)⊆L1(Q)L^2(Q)\subseteq L^1(Q)L2(Q)⊆L1(Q); these facts are used below.

How the Lean proof follows this argument

source_isProbabilityMeasure is an instance of IsProbabilityMeasure (source ι), Mathlib's class asserting that a measure has total mass one. Because it is an instance, the fact is supplied automatically wherever a probability (or finite) measure is required later, for example to form the constant class in L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q) in the expectation identity (5). The proof unfolds the definition (unfold source) and lets infer_instance find Mathlib's instance stating that Measure.infinitePi of probability measures is a probability measure, together with the instance stating that gaussianReal 0 1 is a probability measure.

03Each coordinate has the standard Gaussian law §

Mathematical statement and proof

For a function X:Ω→RX:\Omega\to\mathbb RX:Ω→R and a probability measure μ\muμ on R\mathbb RR, we say that XXX has law μ\muμ under QQQ if XXX is measurable up to a QQQ-null set and its image measure X#QX_\#QX#​Q, defined by X#Q(A)=Q(X−1(A))X_\#Q(A)=Q(X^{-1}(A))X#​Q(A)=Q(X−1(A)) for Borel sets A⊆RA\subseteq\mathbb RA⊆R, equals μ\muμ.

Claim. For every i∈ιi\in\iotai∈ι, the coordinate ξi(ω)=ωi\xi_i(\omega)=\omega_iξi​(ω)=ωi​ is measurable and has law N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1) under QQQ.

Proof. The coordinate maps are measurable by the definition of the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra. For a Borel set A⊆RA\subseteq\mathbb RA⊆R, the preimage ξi−1(A)={ω:ωi∈A}\xi_i^{-1}(A)=\{\omega:\omega_i\in A\}ξi−1​(A)={ω:ωi​∈A} is the set on the left of (1) with F={i}F=\{i\}F={i} and Ai=AA_i=AAi​=A. Therefore

(ξi)#Q(A)=Q({ω:ωi∈A})=N(0,1)(A).(\xi_i)_\#Q(A)=Q(\{\omega:\omega_i\in A\})=\mathcal N(0,1)(A).(ξi​)#​Q(A)=Q({ω:ωi​∈A})=N(0,1)(A).

Since AAA was an arbitrary Borel set, (ξi)#Q=N(0,1)(\xi_i)_\#Q=\mathcal N(0,1)(ξi​)#​Q=N(0,1). □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument

Mathlib's HasLaw X μ P is a structure with two fields: almost-everywhere measurability of X with respect to P, and the identity P.map X = μ, where P.map X is the image measure X#PX_\#PX#​P. The proof of coordinate_hasLaw is an anonymous constructor ⟨…, …⟩ providing the two fields. The first is (measurable_pi_apply i).aemeasurable: evaluation at i is measurable for the product σ\sigmaσ-algebra, hence almost everywhere measurable. The second is Measure.infinitePi_map_eval _ i, Mathlib's marginal identity for product measures: the image of Measure.infinitePi μ under evaluation at i is the factor μ i, here gaussianReal 0 1.

04The coordinate as a square-integrable class §

Mathematical statement and proof

Recall that L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q) is the space of equivalence classes of measurable functions X:Ω→RX:\Omega\to\mathbb RX:Ω→R with ∫X2 dQ<∞\int X^2\,dQ<\infty∫X2dQ<∞, two functions being identified when they agree QQQ-almost everywhere. With the inner product ⟨X,Y⟩=∫XY dQ\langle X,Y\rangle=\int XY\,dQ⟨X,Y⟩=∫XYdQ and the norm ∥X∥2=⟨X,X⟩1/2\|X\|_2=\langle X,X\rangle^{1/2}∥X∥2​=⟨X,X⟩1/2 it is a real Hilbert space; completeness is the Riesz–Fischer theorem.

Claim and definition. For every i∈ιi\in\iotai∈ι, ∫ξi2 dQ<∞\int\xi_i^2\,dQ<\infty∫ξi2​dQ<∞. We write Zi∈L2(Q)Z_i\in L^2(Q)Zi​∈L2(Q) for the class of ξi\xi_iξi​.

Proof. For every nonnegative Borel function fff on R\mathbb RR, the change-of-variables formula for image measures gives ∫f(ξi) dQ=∫f d(ξi)#Q\int f(\xi_i)\,dQ=\int f\,d(\xi_i)_\#Q∫f(ξi​)dQ=∫fd(ξi​)#​Q: for indicators of Borel sets this is the definition of the image measure, for nonnegative simple functions it follows by linearity, and for general fff by monotone convergence. With f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2f(x)=x2 and the previous step,

∫Ωξi2 dQ=∫Rx2 N(0,1)(dx)=12π∫Rx2e−x2/2 dx.\int_\Omega\xi_i^2\,dQ=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}x^2e^{-x^2/2}\,dx.∫Ω​ξi2​dQ=∫R​x2N(0,1)(dx)=2π​1​∫R​x2e−x2/2dx.

The last integral is finite: the function x↦x2e−x2/4x\mapsto x^2e^{-x^2/4}x↦x2e−x2/4 attains its maximum 4/e4/e4/e at x2=4x^2=4x2=4, so x2e−x2/2≤(4/e) e−x2/4x^2e^{-x^2/2}\le(4/e)\,e^{-x^2/4}x2e−x2/2≤(4/e)e−x2/4, and ∫e−x2/4 dx=2π\int e^{-x^2/4}\,dx=2\sqrt\pi∫e−x2/4dx=2π​. (Its exact value 111 is computed in ULA-SC, Section 3.6.8.) □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument

MemLp f p μ is Mathlib's statement that f is almost everywhere strongly measurable and ∫∣f∣p dμ<∞\int|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty∫∣f∣pdμ<∞. Lp ℝ 2 (source ι) is the space L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q) of almost-everywhere classes, which Mathlib equips with the norm ∥X∥2\|X\|_2∥X∥2​ and the inner product ∫XY dQ\int XY\,dQ∫XYdQ. The definition coordinateLp obtains the membership in two steps: memLp_id_gaussianReal (2 : ℝ≥0) states that the identity function belongs to L2L^2L2 of a real Gaussian law, and (coordinate_hasLaw i).memLp transfers this through the law of the coordinate, which is the change of variables of the proof. Then .toLp (fun ω ↦ ω i) forms the class of ξi\xi_iξi​ in Lp ℝ 2 (source ι).

05The coordinate class is represented by the coordinate §

Mathematical statement and proof

Claim. For every i∈ιi\in\iotai∈ι, every representative of the class ZiZ_iZi​ agrees with ξi\xi_iξi​ outside a QQQ-null set; that is, Zi(ω)=ωiZ_i(\omega)=\omega_iZi​(ω)=ωi​ for QQQ-almost every ω\omegaω.

Proof. ZiZ_iZi​ is by definition the class of ξi\xi_iξi​, and two functions belong to the same class exactly when they agree almost everywhere. □\square□

Functions that agree almost everywhere have the same integral and the same image measure. Hence integrals, laws and almost-sure statements about ZiZ_iZi​ may be computed with ξi\xi_iξi​ in place of ZiZ_iZi​.

How the Lean proof follows this argument

An element of Lp is an equivalence class. Lean coerces it to a function by choosing a strongly measurable representative, so that coordinateLp i ω denotes the value of that representative at ω\omegaω. The notation f =ᵐ[μ] g means f(ω)=g(ω)f(\omega)=g(\omega)f(ω)=g(ω) for μ\muμ-almost every ω\omegaω. The proof of coordinateLp_coe is Mathlib's lemma coeFn_toLp (the chosen representative of the class formed by toLp agrees almost everywhere with the original function), applied to the membership proof used in coordinateLp.

06Independence of the coordinates §

Mathematical statement and proof

Recall that a family (Xi)i∈ι(X_i)_{i\in\iota}(Xi​)i∈ι​ of real random variables is independent under QQQ if for every finite set F⊆ιF\subseteq\iotaF⊆ι and all Borel sets Ai⊆RA_i\subseteq\mathbb RAi​⊆R (i∈Fi\in Fi∈F),

Q(⋂i∈F{Xi∈Ai})=∏i∈FQ({Xi∈Ai}).Q\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in F}\{X_i\in A_i\}\Bigr)=\prod_{i\in F}Q(\{X_i\in A_i\}).Q(i∈F⋂​{Xi​∈Ai​})=i∈F∏​Q({Xi​∈Ai​}).

Claim. The coordinates (ξi)i∈ι(\xi_i)_{i\in\iota}(ξi​)i∈ι​ are independent under QQQ.

Proof. Fix a finite set FFF and Borel sets AiA_iAi​, i∈Fi\in Fi∈F. The intersection ⋂i∈F{ξi∈Ai}\bigcap_{i\in F}\{\xi_i\in A_i\}⋂i∈F​{ξi​∈Ai​} is the set {ω:ωi∈Ai for all i∈F}\{\omega:\omega_i\in A_i\text{ for all }i\in F\}{ω:ωi​∈Ai​ for all i∈F}, so by (1) its measure is ∏i∈FN(0,1)(Ai)\prod_{i\in F}\mathcal N(0,1)(A_i)∏i∈F​N(0,1)(Ai​). By the law of the coordinates (ULA-SC, Section 3.6.3), N(0,1)(Ai)=Q({ξi∈Ai})\mathcal N(0,1)(A_i)=Q(\{\xi_i\in A_i\})N(0,1)(Ai​)=Q({ξi​∈Ai​}) for each iii, which gives the product formula. □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument

iIndepFun X μ is Mathlib's mutual independence of a family of random variables: for every finite set of indices, events taken from the σ\sigmaσ-algebras generated by the corresponding variables have the product property displayed above. The events in the σ\sigmaσ-algebra generated by ξi\xi_iξi​ are exactly the sets {ξi∈A}\{\xi_i\in A\}{ξi​∈A} with AAA Borel, so this is the definition recalled in the claim. The proof is Mathlib's iIndepFun_infinitePi: on a product measure Measure.infinitePi P, the variables ω↦Xi(ωi)\omega\mapsto X_i(\omega_i)ω↦Xi​(ωi​) are independent for any measurable maps XiX_iXi​. Here every XiX_iXi​ is the identity, measurable by measurable_id.

07Each coordinate has mean zero §

Mathematical statement and proof

Claim. For every i∈ιi\in\iotai∈ι,

∫Ωωi Q(dω)=0.\int_\Omega\omega_i\,Q(d\omega)=0.∫Ω​ωi​Q(dω)=0.

Proof. The change-of-variables formula of ULA-SC, Section 3.6.4 gives ∫∣ξi∣ dQ=∫∣x∣ N(0,1)(dx)=2/π<∞\int|\xi_i|\,dQ=\int|x|\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)=\sqrt{2/\pi}<\infty∫∣ξi​∣dQ=∫∣x∣N(0,1)(dx)=2/π​<∞, so ξi\xi_iξi​ is integrable. Applying the same formula to the positive and negative parts of the identity function,

∫Ωξi dQ=∫Rx N(0,1)(dx)=12π∫Rx e−x2/2 dx=0.\int_\Omega\xi_i\,dQ=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}x\,e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=0.∫Ω​ξi​dQ=∫R​xN(0,1)(dx)=2π​1​∫R​xe−x2/2dx=0.

The last integral vanishes because the integrand is integrable and odd: the substitution x↦−xx\mapsto-xx↦−x shows that the integral equals its own negative. □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument

The proof applies Mathlib's change of variables for a random variable with a given law, (coordinate_hasLaw i).integral_comp, which states ∫f(X) dP=∫f dμ\int f(X)\,dP=\int f\,d\mu∫f(X)dP=∫fdμ when XXX has law μ\muμ under PPP and fff is almost everywhere strongly measurable. Here f := id, and the measurability side condition is measurable_id.aestronglyMeasurable. The resulting identity ∫ξi dQ=∫x N(0,1)(dx)\int\xi_i\,dQ=\int x\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)∫ξi​dQ=∫xN(0,1)(dx) is chained by .trans with integral_id_gaussianReal, Mathlib's formula ∫x N(m,v)(dx)=m\int x\,\mathcal N(m,v)(dx)=m∫xN(m,v)(dx)=m, here with m=0m=0m=0. Mathlib's integral is the Bochner integral, which is defined for every function and agrees with the Lebesgue integral on integrable functions; the change of variables holds without an integrability hypothesis, so the integrability shown in the proof does not appear as a separate input.

08Inner products of the coordinate classes §

Mathematical statement and proof

Claim. For all i,j∈ιi,j\in\iotai,j∈ι,

⟨Zi,Zj⟩L2(Q)={1,i=j,0,i≠j.\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle_{L^2(Q)}=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j.\end{cases}⟨Zi​,Zj​⟩L2(Q)​={1,0,​i=j,i=j.​

Proof. By definition of the inner product of L2(Q)L^2(Q)L2(Q), ⟨Zi,Zj⟩=∫ZiZj dQ\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle=\int Z_iZ_j\,dQ⟨Zi​,Zj​⟩=∫Zi​Zj​dQ, computed with any representatives. By ULA-SC, Section 3.6.5 there are QQQ-null sets NiN_iNi​ and NjN_jNj​ outside which Zi=ξiZ_i=\xi_iZi​=ξi​ and Zj=ξjZ_j=\xi_jZj​=ξj​, respectively. Outside the null set Ni∪NjN_i\cup N_jNi​∪Nj​ we have ZiZj=ξiξjZ_iZ_j=\xi_i\xi_jZi​Zj​=ξi​ξj​, and functions that agree almost everywhere have the same integral. Hence

⟨Zi,Zj⟩=∫Ωωi ωj Q(dω).(2)\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle=\int_\Omega\omega_i\,\omega_j\,Q(d\omega).\qquad(2)⟨Zi​,Zj​⟩=∫Ω​ωi​ωj​Q(dω).(2)

Case i=ji=ji=j. By the change of variables of ULA-SC, Section 3.6.4 through the law N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1) of ξi\xi_iξi​,

∫Ωωi2 Q(dω)=∫Rx2 N(0,1)(dx)=1.\int_\Omega\omega_i^2\,Q(d\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)=1.∫Ω​ωi2​Q(dω)=∫R​x2N(0,1)(dx)=1.

Here we used that the second moment of N(0,v)\mathcal N(0,v)N(0,v) equals vvv, since its mean is 000 and its variance is vvv (see ULA-SC, Section 3.4.1); in the present case v=1v=1v=1.

Case i≠ji\ne ji=j. The coordinates ξi\xi_iξi​ and ξj\xi_jξj​ are independent (ULA-SC, Section 3.6.6), and both are integrable with mean zero (ULA-SC, Section 3.6.7). For two independent integrable real random variables the product is integrable and its expectation is the product of the expectations. Therefore

∫Ωωi ωj Q(dω)=(∫Ωωi Q(dω))(∫Ωωj Q(dω))=0⋅0=0.\int_\Omega\omega_i\,\omega_j\,Q(d\omega)=\Bigl(\int_\Omega\omega_i\,Q(d\omega)\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_\Omega\omega_j\,Q(d\omega)\Bigr)=0\cdot0=0.∫Ω​ωi​ωj​Q(dω)=(∫Ω​ωi​Q(dω))(∫Ω​ωj​Q(dω))=0⋅0=0.

Combining the two cases with (2) proves the claim. □\square□

How the Lean proof follows this argument
  1. rw [L2.inner_def] rewrites the inner product of two classes as ∫⟨Zi(ω),Zj(ω)⟩ Q(dω)\int\langle Z_i(\omega),Z_j(\omega)\rangle\,Q(d\omega)∫⟨Zi​(ω),Zj​(ω)⟩Q(dω); the integrand is the inner product of two real numbers, that is, their product.
  2. heq states that this integrand equals ωiωj\omega_i\omega_jωi​ωj​ almost everywhere. partial_sum_coe takes an arbitrary function a : ι → ℝ and a finite set s : Finset ι. The proof is induction s using Finset.induction_on, induction on finite sets by insertion of one new element.

  1. In the empty case, Lp.coeFn_zero states that the representative of the zero class vanishes almost everywhere, and simpa only [Finset.sum_empty, Pi.zero_apply] identifies both empty sums with 000.
  2. In the insert case the new element is i, his states that it is not in s, and ih is the induction hypothesis. Finset.sum_insert his splits off the term of i. 26The covariance of two isonormal variables §

Mathematical statement and proof

For real random variables X,Y∈L2(Q)X,Y\in L^2(Q)X,Y∈L2(Q), the covariance is Cov⁡(X,Y)=∫Ω(X−∫X dQ)(Y−∫Y dQ) dQ\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\int_\Omega\bigl(X-\int X\,dQ\bigr)\bigl(Y-\int Y\,dQ\bigr)\,dQCov(X,Y)=∫Ω​(X−∫XdQ)(Y−∫YdQ)dQ.

Claim. For all x,y∈Hx,y\in Hx,y∈H, Cov⁡(Ib(x),Ib(y))=⟨x,y⟩H\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(I_b(x),I_b(y)\bigr)=\langle x,y\rangle_HCov(Ib​(x),Ib​(y))=⟨x,y⟩H​.

Proof. Both means vanish (ULA-SC, Section 3.6.17), so

Cov⁡(Ib(x),Ib(y))=∫ΩIb(x) Ib(y) dQ=⟨Ib(x),Ib(y)⟩L2(Q).\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(I_b(x),I_b(y)\bigr)=\int_\Omega I_b(x)\,I_b(y)\,dQ=\langle I_b(x),I_b(y)\rangle_{L^2(Q)}.Cov(Ib​(x),Ib​(y))=∫Ω​Ib​(x)Ib​(y)dQ=⟨Ib​(x),Ib​(y)⟩L2(Q)​.

In every real inner product space, expanding ∥u±v∥2=∥u∥2±2⟨u,v⟩+∥v∥2\|u\pm v\|^2=\|u\|^2\pm2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2∥u±v∥2=∥u∥2±2⟨u,v⟩+∥v∥2 gives the polarization identity ⟨u,v⟩=14(∥u+v∥2−∥u−v∥2)\langle u,v\rangle=\frac14\bigl(\|u+v\|^2-\|u-v\|^2\bigr)⟨u,v⟩=41​(∥u+v∥2−∥u−v∥2). By linearity, Ib(x)±Ib(y)=Ib(x±y)I_b(x)\pm I_b(y)=I_b(x\pm y)Ib​(x)±Ib​(y)=Ib​(x±y), and IbI_bIb​ preserves norms (ULA-SC, Section 3.6.12). Therefore

⟨Ib(x),Ib(y)⟩=14(∥Ib(x+y)∥22−∥Ib(x−y)∥22)=14(∥x+y∥2−∥x−y∥2)=⟨x,y⟩.\langle I_b(x),I_b(y)\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|I_b(x+y)\|_2^2-\|I_b(x-y)\|_2^2\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)=\langle x,y\rangle.⟨Ib​(x),Ib​(y)⟩=41​(∥Ib​(x+y)∥22​−∥Ib​(x−y)∥22​)=41​(∥x+y∥2−∥x−y∥2)=⟨x,y⟩.

□\square□

For y=xy=xy=x this gives Var⁡(Ib(x))=∥x∥2\operatorname{Var}(I_b(x))=\|x\|^2Var(Ib​(x))=∥x∥2, the variance found in ULA-SC, Section 3.6.24.

How the Lean proof follows this argument

cov[X, Y; μ] is Mathlib's covariance, defined as ∫(X−EX)(Y−EY) dμ\int(X-\mathbb EX)(Y-\mathbb EY)\,d\mu∫(X−EX)(Y−EY)dμ; unfold covariance exposes this definition. The rewrites with isonormal_mean (twice) and sub_zero remove the means. rw [← (isonormal b).inner_map_map] replaces ⟨x,y⟩\langle x,y\rangle⟨x,y⟩ by ⟨Ib(x),Ib(y)⟩\langle I_b(x),I_b(y)\rangle⟨Ib​(x),Ib​(y)⟩; Mathlib's inner_map_map for a linear isometry is proved by the polarization identity, as in the argument above. Finally L2.inner_def writes the inner product as an integral, and integral_congr_ae with filter_upwards with ω and simp [mul_comm] identifies the two integrands pointwise.
